findings.source_passage: She remembered the proverb about the good dying young, I suppose. There must be a certain amount of original sin in me to have survived.
findings.source_locator: Early dialogue exchange, after 'Who thought I was dead? / Tuppence.'
findings.why_it_matters: This is a character-defining wisecrack that establishes Tommy's self-deprecating wit under pressure; it is the kind of distinctively voiced aside Christie deploys to mark her protagonists' resilience. Its absence flattens the reunion scene.
findings.suggested_fix: Restore Tommy's line verbatim in the dialogue exchange immediately after Julius names Tuppence as the one who feared him dead.

findings.source_passage: I was in such a funk I had to think of something,
source_locator": "After Julius praises Tommy's bluff — 'How you ever came to think of it all so pat beats me to a frazzle!'
findings.why_it_matters: This self-deprecating one-liner is the rhetorical pay-off to Julius's enthusiastic praise and is tonally signature Christie — the hero deflating his own heroism with disarming plainness. Its omission removes a small but distinctive beat.
findings.suggested_fix: Restore the exchange: Julius's 'beats me to a frazzle' praise followed immediately by Tommy's 'I was in such a funk I had to think of something,' said Tommy simply.

findings.source_passage: Tommy was filled with a passionate and utterly illogical resentment. It was all very well to say things like that—but a real girl would never marry for money. Tuppence was utterly cold-blooded and selfish, and he would be delighted if he never saw her again! And it was a rotten world!
findings.source_locator: Interior monologue paragraph beginning 'Tuppence and Julius! Well, why not?'
findings.why_it_matters: This interior passage is the interpretive crux of the Tommy/Tuppence romance arc in the chapter: it reveals Tommy's true feelings through his illogical jealousy and is written with the ironic free-indirect voice Christie uses for comic romantic tension. The draft jumps straight from 'gee along together very well' to Tommy demanding to see the note, skipping the emotional core entirely.
findings.suggested_fix: Restore the free-indirect interior monologue in full between Julius's 'We ought to gee along together very well' and Tommy's demand to see the letter; this is interpretively essential to the romance subplot and cannot be compressed away without loss.

findings.source_passage: Tommy handed it back, his eyes shining... Had she not refused Julius without hesitation? True, the note betokened signs of weakening, but he could excuse that... Darling Tuppence, there was not a girl in the world to touch her!
findings.source_locator: Paragraph immediately following Tommy reading Tuppence's note
findings.why_it_matters: The draft reduces this to 'Tommy's eyes shone. Darling Tuppence!' — a single sentence vs. a sustained ironic free-indirect reversal. The comic logic of Tommy's 'sharp reaction' (going from resentment to adoration on the evidence of one ambiguous note) is the emotional and tonal signature of the scene; collapsing it to a fragment erases the irony.
findings.suggested_fix: Expand the passage after Tommy reads the note to include his rationalisation ('True, the note betokened signs of weakening, but he could excuse that') and the ironic 'Darling Tuppence, there was not a girl in the world to touch her!' in something close to the source rhythm.

findings.source_passage: We've been like a couple of babes playing 'Here we go round the Mulberry Bush.' Now I'm going right along to Scotland Yard to ask them to take me by the hand and show me the way I should go.
findings.source_locator: Julius's speech proposing they go to Scotland Yard
findings.why_it_matters: This nursery-rhyme metaphor is the most rhetorically distinctive phrase in Julius's speech and gives his self-critique vivid comic colour; it is precisely the kind of Americanised exuberance that defines Julius's voice. The draft retains the gist but drops the line entirely.
findings.suggested_fix: Restore Julius's 'couple of babes playing Here we go round the Mulberry Bush' line in his Scotland Yard speech.

findings.source_passage: Henry gasped and spoke… 'She crumpled it up into a ball and threw it into the grate, and made a sort of noise like "Whoop!" sir.'
findings.source_locator: The page-boy Henry's final speech, just before Tommy tips him
findings.why_it_matters: The detail 'made a sort of noise like Whoop!' is a small but charming piece of comic characterisation (Tuppence's irrepressible energy glimpsed through the page-boy's eyes) and is tonally distinctive. The draft keeps only 'crumpled it into a ball and threw it into the grate,' dropping the exclamation.
findings.suggested_fix: Add 'and made a sort of noise like Whoop, sir' to the page-boy's account to preserve the comic texture.

summary: The draft omits Tommy's jealousy interior monologue (the romantic arc's interpretive keystone), flattens the ironic free-indirect reversal after he reads Tuppence's note, and drops several distinctively voiced lines (Tommy's 'original sin' quip, his 'in such a funk' deflation, Julius's Mulberry Bush metaphor), collectively constituting four medium-severity failures that together trigger regeneration.
